slides.title: Why did Tudor families need their children's help?
slides.lead: Every home needs food, a fire and a roof, every single day.

lines.value: In Tudor times there were no shops on the corner, and no light switches on the walls.

slides.speakerNotes:
Say to children: Think about your home. What does it need every single day? Food. A fire to cook on and keep warm. Somewhere to sleep. Now we're going back to Tudor England, between 1485 and 1603. That's after the Romans and long before the Victorians. Look at this farm. No shop on the corner. No switch on the wall, no electricity at all. So everything a home needed had to come from somewhere, and somebody had to go and get it.

Teacher information: The picture is a modern reconstruction, not a photograph of a real Tudor child; the caption says so.

slides.title: Why did Tudor families need their children's help?
lines:
If you needed wood, somebody had to fetch it.
Wheat had to be carried in by hand.
Look at her. She isn't being paid to do this.
slides.question: How does carrying those sticks help her family?
slides.sticky: Many Tudor children helped their households get food, fuel or money.
slides.speakerNotes:
Say to children: If you wanted a fire tonight, somebody went and fetched the wood. If you wanted bread, somebody cut the wheat and carried it in. All of it by hand. Now look at her. What's she carrying? Sticks. What are they for? The fire, for cooking. Nobody is paying her a penny for this, but tonight the family eats because of what's in her arms. So how does carrying those sticks help her family? That's why Tudor children worked: the house needed doing, and everyone who could, helped.

Teacher information: Facts follow the supplied Lesson 2 and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust's A Day in the Life of a Tudor.

slides.title: What did a Tudor apprentice get?

lead.value: Some Tudor children left home to learn a trade from someone called a master.

lines: Look: the master shows, and the boy copies.

lines.value: That's how Tudor apprentices learned a trade: by working next to someone who could, often for seven years.

slides.speakerNotes:
Say to children: Not every Tudor child worked at home. Some left home to live with a master and learn a trade: making shoes, baking bread, sewing clothes. Look at this workshop. The master is showing, and the boy is copying. That's how you learned a trade in Tudor times, by doing it next to someone who could, day after day. It usually took about seven years.

Teacher information: Modern summary: Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, The Tudor Apprentice, pages 1 to 2. The craft is illustrative, not a record of a named apprentice.

slides.title: What did a Tudor apprentice get?

lines.value:
This was the deal.
The apprentice worked for the master.
The master gave him food, clothes and a bed.
He wasn't paid.

slides.question: So what did an apprentice get out of it?
slides.sticky: An apprenticeship could provide food and a home now, and a way to earn a living later.
slides.speakerNotes:
Say to children: Here's how the deal worked. The apprentice worked for the master. In return, the master gave him his food, his clothes and a bed to sleep in. No wages. So what did an apprentice get out of it? Two things. Straight away, he was fed and he had a roof over his head. And later, once he could make a shoe that fitted and lasted, he could earn his own living. Two different reasons, and one apprenticeship gave both.

Teacher information: Modern summary: Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, The Tudor Apprentice, pages 1 to 2.

slides.title: Why keep working when it was hard?
slides.question: So why would a Tudor family still choose this for their child?
lines: It had a hard side. Long days, strict rules and little free time. Some masters were kind, and some were not.

lines.value: But most Tudor children couldn't go to school.
The family needed what the deal gave: food now, and a trade for later. Even families with money paid for it.

slides.speakerNotes:
Say to children: Now, I'm not going to pretend this was easy. The days were long. The rules were strict. There wasn't much free time. Some masters looked after their apprentices well, and some treated them badly. So here's my question. Why would a Tudor family still choose this for their child? Were they cruel? No. Think about what else there was. Most Tudor children couldn't go to school at all. And the family needed what the deal gave them: the child fed and housed now, and a trade to earn a living with later. Even families with plenty of money paid for an apprenticeship, because a trade was that valuable. So when we explain why Tudor children worked, we explain it with what life was like then, not with what we've got now.

Teacher information: Conditions: Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, The Tudor Apprentice, pages 1 to 2. Schooling context follows the supplied plan. Do not infer treatment or hours from the reconstruction.
